title: Ashtpadi 12, salok: the humble

cards: Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. Heads are covered. And if you stay, you sit on the floor.
No pews, no front-row chairs, no reserved seats for donors. A surgeon sits beside a taxi driver; a grandmother beside a teenager who came straight from practice.
One thing in the room is raised: the Guru Granth Sahib, on its platform under a canopy. Everyone else is at the same height, and it's low. That floor is a lesson before anyone says a word.
Today the salok of the twelfth ashtpadi says it out loud.

teach.b: The salok's two lines lean against each other. The first, in Guru Arjan's words: sukhee basai maskeeneeaa, aap nivaar tale. The meek one dwells in peace, having set the self down low.
The second is the mirror: the great, great proud ones, Nanak, are worn away by their own pride.

The Punjabi word for humility is nimrataa, and the salok's maskeen is its close cousin: the meek one, who claims nothing. Notice the verb, nivaar: to push aside, to remove. Humility here isn't feeling worthless.

teach.h: SET THE SELF DOWN, LIKE A BAG.
teach.b: You take the loud, insisting self and set it down, like a heavy bag at the door. The result is sukh, ease, the same sukh in Sukhmani's own name, so this salok sits close to the heart of the hymn.
Why would lowering yourself bring ease? Look at what pride costs. It needs defending.
It has to win the argument, get the credit, be seen at the right height. The proud person is always on guard duty; the humble one has put the guard down.

teach.h: NO SEAT TO BE KNOCKED FROM.
teach.b: Nobody can knock you off a seat you never climbed onto.

The gurdwara floor, and the langar rows where people eat side by side, can be read as this salok made physical. Nobody earns a higher place there. And the salok puts the peace exactly there: in the sitting down.

how: In a gurdwara everyone sits on the floor at the same height, with only the Guru Granth Sahib raised, and in the langar people eat side by side in rows; Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach this salok at the opening of the twelfth ashtpadi.

o: feeling that you are worth nothing
humility: setting the self down low
politeness shown to elders and guests

games.q: the salok of the humble — tap the pairs.
p: the meek one, who claims nothing

s: in Sukhmani, humility means thinking you are worthless
nivaar is an action: you set the loud self down, like a heavy bag.
in a gurdwara, only the Guru Granth Sahib is raised; everyone else sits on the floor
no pews, no reserved seats: the same low floor for all.
the salok promises the proud a peaceful life
its second line says the proud are worn away by their own pride.

games.q: you walk into a gurdwara for the first time. where do you sit?
o: in a chair near the front.
on the floor, with everyone else.
games.why: on the floor. only the Guru Granth Sahib is raised; donors and newcomers sit at the same low height.

practice: If you can, sit on the floor for these two minutes; if not, lower your shoulders and let your chin drop a little.

Picture the self as a bag you've been carrying, your reputation, your need to be right, and set it down beside you; you can pick it up later. For now, just sit low and notice whether anything gets easier.

wordCard.voice: Nimrataa. Humility: not thinking less of yourself, but setting the self down, low, the way the salok's meek one does. The salok promises that person peace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nimrataa, humility; the salok itself uses maskeen, the meek one.

carryVoice: Your line: the humble rest easy. The guard can go off duty now, and the floor holds you. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 12, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278)
